lessons.title: Why and when we prune
lessons.html:
What is pruning?

Pruning means cutting away certain branches of a tree on purpose. On deciduous fruit trees, such as apples, pears, peaches, nectarines, plums and apricots, pruning is one of the most important jobs of the year.

Why we prune

  • To give the tree a good shape that is strong and easy to work in.
  • To let sunlight and air into the tree. Fruit in the sun gets better colour and sugar, and diseases spread less where air moves.
  • To keep a balance between growth and fruit, so the tree carries good-sized fruit every year.
  • To remove dead, diseased, broken or crossing branches.
  • To keep the tree at a height that pickers can reach.

When we prune

Winter pruning is done when the trees are dormant and have no leaves, usually from June to August in the Western Cape. It is easy to see the shape of the tree. Summer pruning is lighter and removes strong upright water shoots to let in light and slow growth.

Know the wood

Different fruit types carry fruit on different wood. For example, apples and pears carry much of their fruit on spurs, short stubby shoots that live for several years. Peaches and nectarines bear on one-year-old shoots, so new shoots must be renewed each year. Your supervisor will show you how each block must be pruned.

Tree shapes

Common training systems include the central leader, the open vase and various trellis systems. Each farm and block has its own system. Always ask which system is used before you start a new block.

lessons.title: Making good cuts safely
lessons.html:
Tools

  • Secateurs (hand pruners) for thin shoots.
  • Loppers with long handles for thicker branches.
  • Pruning saw for big branches.
  • A sharpening stone and a disinfectant if the farm uses one between trees or blocks.

Keep tools sharp and clean. Blunt tools crush and tear wood, and wounds heal badly.

Two basic cuts

CutWhat you doResult
Thinning cutRemove a whole shoot or branch back to where it startsOpens the tree to light
Heading cutShorten a shoot back to a budMakes several new shoots grow below the cut

Making a good cut

  1. Cut just above an outward-facing bud, at a slight slope away from the bud, so the new shoot grows outwards.
  2. Do not leave long stubs. They die back and let in disease.
  3. Do not cut into the collar (the swollen ring where a branch joins a bigger branch). Cut just outside it.
  4. For heavy branches, use three cuts: an undercut first, then a top cut further out to drop the branch, then a clean final cut at the collar. This stops the bark tearing.

What to remove first

Remove dead, diseased and broken wood first, then branches that cross or rub, then strong upright water shoots, then thin the rest as instructed.

Safety

  • Wear gloves and safety glasses; twigs can hit your eyes.
  • Keep your free hand away from the blades.
  • Use ladders on firm ground and never stand on the top step.
  • Carry tools closed, and never leave a saw lying in the grass.

Pruned wood is usually taken out of the rows and chipped or removed, so it does not spread disease.

Key points

  • Pruning shapes the tree, lets in light and balances growth and fruit.
  • Winter pruning is done when trees are dormant.
  • Thinning cuts remove whole shoots; heading cuts shorten shoots.
  • Cut above an outward bud, leave no stubs and do not cut into the collar.
  • Keep tools sharp and wear gloves and safety glasses.
